chunks: 34 - Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar said: I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Regarding a man who bought a piece of land from another man with its four boundaries, and in it there was crops, palm trees, and other trees, but he did not mention the palm trees, nor the crops, nor the trees in his deed, and he mentioned in it that he had bought it with all its rights, both those inside it and those outside it: Do the palm trees, trees, and crops fall under the rights of the land or not?
So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'When one purchases the land with its boundaries and what is enclosed by its door, then all that is in it belongs to him, if God wills.'
ai.seo_question: Are crops and trees included in a land sale if not explicitly mentioned in the contract?
ai.summary: Recorded by Shaykh al-Tusi in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this narration from Imam al-Hassan al-Askari clarifies the principle of 'inclusion by enclosure' (al-muqabbad) in property transactions, establishing that unlisted assets like crops and trees are automatically transferred with the land if the deed specifies 'all rights.' This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the literal boundaries and physical enclosure of a property as the definitive scope of ownership, preventing disputes over omitted items. It serves as a foundational precedent for modern real estate contracts where specific inventory lists are not exhaustive.
